speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, under standing order 26, to move the adjournment of the house to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance.
The motion is as follows:
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) the adjournment of the house to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the suspension of winter works in several municipalities in the Province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, this is a question-

speechtext:

subtopic: WINTER WORKS, QUEBEC-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel my motion meets every requirement of the standing orders, since it is a very definite matter, that is, the suspension of winter works which

January 19, 1966
Labour Conditions
were stopped because the amounts appropriated for carrying out the 1964-65 works by the federal and provincial governments have not yet been paid, thus restricting the credit facilities of municipalities which were unable to borrow the required amounts for the 1965-66 works. As a result, the works for the current season have been suspended.
Such is the specific purpose of my motion. The matter is important. First, because we find that the statute governing winter works has become inoperative; second, it is an important matter since it is impossible to know which government, the federal or the provincial, is responsible for the delay in payments for winter works that were carried out two years ago; third, it is also an important problem because this seems to happen only in the province of Quebec-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: WINTER WORKS, QUEBEC-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but he must, at this time, limit his remarks to the matter of the urgency and not to that of the importance of the issue he would like to have debated.

subtopic: WINTER WORKS, QUEBEC-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, here is why the problem is urgent:
First, with each passing day thousands of Canadians in many municipalities are deprived of their livelihood and are thus prevented from enjoying a minimum standard of living in Canada.
Second, in order to point out the urgency of the problem with which we are concerned today, I ask for the support of the new Minister of Manpower for the workers who are most in need, those who have lost their jobs and are waiting for winter works in order to obtain the necessities of life-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: WINTER WORKS, QUEBEC-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Lapointe knows, we should at this time consider, not the importance of the question he raises, but the urgency of the debate.
I would ask him to refer to section 100 (3), in Beauchesne, which reads as follows:
"Urgency" within this rule does not apply to the matter itself, but it means "urgency of debate", when the ordinary opportunities provided iby the rules of the House do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough and public interest demands that discussion take place immediately.
There is no doubt that the question raised by the hon. member for Lapointe is very important, but I should like to remind him that he will have an opportunity to discuss it during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne.

In the circumstances I do not feel that it would be possible for me to accept a motion for the adjournment of the current business of the house at this time.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY MOVED BY MR. J. P. GOYER AND SECONDED BY MR. ROBERT STANBURY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to congratulate you on your election and to express the hope that the qualities you have shown in the past will remain with you in the discharge of your new duties. I have not had the chance to get to know you very well yet, but you certainly have every reason to be proud of the reputation you have made for yourself among the members of this house. To prove it, I have only to recall the support you received yesterday.
I had been told that discussions in this house often were long and hard. Perhaps I may be allowed to question such an assertion, in view of the fact that, since yesterday, all motions have been accepted with an amazing degree of unanimity and dispatch. But now I feel a bit reassured, if I may put it that way. The question period indicated that, from now on, that unanimity might not be quite so strong.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) for the honour he has extended to the constituents of Dollard in asking me to move the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I should also like to join with my electors in congratulating the Prime Minister for having once again led the Liberal party to victory.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY MOVED BY MR. J. P. GOYER AND SECONDED BY MR. ROBERT STANBURY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY MOVED BY MR. J. P. GOYER AND SECONDED BY MR. ROBERT STANBURY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the last few years, federal-provincial relations, and more particularly, the relations with the province of Quebec have given rise to many problems. Those problems have revived the question of the relations that should exist between French speaking and English speaking Canadians within confederation.
Some people are anchored in extreme positions which greatly threaten to aggravate the situation beyond hope. I loathe those extremists, whether they be French speaking or

DEBATES	January 19, 1966
English speaking Canadians, whether they act openly or prefer to resort to passive resistance, which is just as blameworthy. But that is not enough.
There is in our country a majority of citizens who sincerely hope for the advent of a general consensus and such a majority should normally be represented within the Canadian parliament.
With this majority in mind, the government should without delay take positive action to implement what to this day seemed only desirable. This positive action need not wait for the report of the Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism, nor for the passing of a generation to become operative. Even if new findings require adjustments, the federal government should stay ahead of public opinion and this implies concrete measures.
Already the government has reset in motion-and this time full ahead-the mechanics of federal-provincial conferences. It was high time the federal government realized that the requirements of the war effort could no longer be justified after 20 years.
Hence, the necessity of developing areas of jurisdiction against an obsolete status quo. This proves the necessity of studying together the problems arising from joint jurisdictions. Dialogue has now started; it may be painful but it is sustained. What better proof that negotiation is not abdication, in spite of what some people maintain.
While on that point, Mr. Speaker, let us not any longer believe or encourage the belief that Quebec's claims are always inspired by tenets of isolationism and realize, for a change, that other provinces too are asserting their rights.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
It is becoming increasingly obvious that the provinces are endeavouring to take over management of those fields of jurisdiction which are rightfully theirs and which, the federal government has taken over by setting out its own policies, for lack of appropriate provincial policies and due to the war effort which had drained revenues into the federal coffers.
It is true that the provinces are often better equipped to meet some of the needs of the people. Why then should there be vain struggles, when, in the final analysis, the citizens are the only ones to suffer from the ensuing delays.
For the common good, it is preferable to hand over to the provinces those spheres of
January 19, 1966

jurisdiction, which, at any rate, are theirs under the constitution.
Moreover, French Canada makes sure of having safety-catches, especially in the field of their language and culture, and that is normal.
But, in doing so, they are not advocating isolationism. On the contrary, this action, in my view, reflects the will to have vested rights respected and to claim the means by which those rights can blossom out to benefit national unity.
On the other hand, in matters of joint jurisdiction each government should agree to co-operate closely and constantly.
Let us take the case of the St. Lawrence river, for instance. It has, of course, lost nothing of its majesty over the years but, to-day, its waters are polluted and this spoils any pleasure which the riverside population, particularly the people of Montreal, could enjoy. The province and the municipal governments can certainly help lessen water pollution in the St. Lawrence by providing a sewage disposal plant. But what will the result be if the federal government does not shoulder its responsibilities? It falls to the government to ensure observance of the required sanitary measures all along this river which starts at the Great Lakes.
That is practically a new field of endeavour which calls for concerted action by all levels of government.
What about the Ottawa River, one side of which is polluted by factories while the other is kept clean for summer vacationers?
Many examples could be given to prove beyond doubt the interdependence of the different governments.
Finally, there are matters which fall exclusively under the federal jurisdiction and about which there could not be any agreements with one or more provinces without jeopardizing the national unity and throwing the general interest of the country out of balance.
This does not rule out consultation, always possible and often useful, between governments, but such consultation could not lead to specific agreements without the entire approval of the federal government.
What I deplore is the fact that the federal government has often lacked originality, not above all, in the preparation of new policies, -quite to the contrary-but in the modernization of its existing policies and in the expression of the positions it adopts. We seem to be lulled by red tape and to be delighted by past experiences, in contrast to the dynamic and adaptable nature of a modern government.
The Address-Mr. Goyer
For instance, transportation in general comes within the federal jurisdiction. How come there is hardly more than a start on the co-ordination of the various means of transportation in Canada? While it is not proof in itself, this example could be multiplied and lead to the conclusion that there is, in areas of exclusive federal jurisdiction, room for improvement of current laws and corresponding services and for the elaboration of a new act, and all this for many parliaments to come.
[English1
I should like to refer now to a field which is exclusively federal. The Speech from the Throne contains an announcement concerning a bill to give our country a national anthem, "O Canada". I hope that this debate, relating to a very distinctive sign of our national entity, will be pursued in a constructive manner. Personally, as a French Canadian I have no objection to the preservation of certain ties with the Crown, ties that can be depicted by external signs. I have no objection even if the only reason for this were the recognition of the historical role British institutions played with regard to the survival of the French fact in Canada.
I will add a more fundamental reason. This action would be an appeal to the feeling of mutual understanding which should inspire all of us if we wish to live together as partners. If a number of Canadians deem it necessary to retain certain external signs of attachment to the Crown, we should be ready to accept them. It is my fervent hope that we may show deference to the Crown while accentuating more and more our national identity.

Mr. Speaker, although I have discussed at length the problem of provincial-federal relations and of strictly federal jurisdiction, I would not like to leave hon. members under the impression that this is the only high priority question in Canada. It seems to me equally urgent to adjust our economy to changing conditions and to new techniques, to maintain our continuing growth, to quickly balance the rate of economic development in the various areas of Canada and to restore human dignity to those who wallow in poverty; our responsibility to share in a peace offensive throughout the world and to raise the living standards of the hungry.
Upon reading the second annual report of the Economic Council of Canada, I noticed in

January 19, 1966
The Address-Mr. Goyer particular a recommendation for increased research work in Canada and I quote:
To reach a satisfactory rate of increase in productivity and to improve our competitive position in the world.
At the present time we spend almost $350 million on research in Canada, a quarter of which is allocated to the Department of National Defence. In view of the full amount of the budget, the share granted to the Department of National Defence seems rather surprising to me.
I note that the Speech from the Throne mentions that matter and I quote:
Legislation to encourage research and development, which will enlarge and improve upon the present taxation incentive.
Industries which will take advantage of this tax exemption will direct their research in very precise fields-at least I would think so. That leads me to the following question: Would it not be that we have tried to develop our research and our industries in all fields at the same time, instead of specializing in some of them. Should the applied research done outside of our industries not be specialized in order to develop and improve our finished products.
That, to my mind, would be one way to help our industry, to give additional support to the Development Corporation of Canada, without for all that putting a stop to the inflow of foreign capital. Today research is no longer carried out on a blackboard. Research projects require a lot of personnel and equipment worth millions of dollars which soon becomes obsolete. If we do not concentrate our investments to give our researchers adequate equipment and salaries, we will be running the risk of falling behind the times and of seeing a greater outflow of our scientists toward places with better prospects.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I have been struck by a finding of the Economic Council of Canada concerning the disparity of the average income per capita and by province, in Canada. In 1963, Ontario headed the list with an average income of $2,025, followed by the Western Provinces. Quebec took sixth place with $1,521, followed by the Atlantic provinces, Newfoundland coming last with only $1,009. In other words, there was a gap of 100 per cent between Ontario and Newfoundland.
Considering this discrepancy according to each area, the Atlantic provinces show a discrepancy of 86 per cent as compared to Ontario. This discrepancy has existed with practically no change since 1926.

This is the situation which can be readily described as tragic and unacceptable. This is a challenge which we have to accept. And this must be possible.
In the United States, the difference in income per capita by area shows only a discrepancy of 55 per cent between the Far East and the Southeast; this discrepancy was more than two times greater in 1929. Hence a significant improvement. It must be noted that this gain was recorded mainly in the immediate post-war period.
To correct this situation we should authorize large investments. The wealthy provinces should agree to help those with low incomes. This is the price of our unity; it is a rule of social justice.
Is it possible not to make brief mention of the announcement by the government concerning the creation of the Department of Manpower under the direction of the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Marchand). A few days ago we were informed of the development of the allowances programs for the training of unemployed workers or handicapped persons, a generous plan to complete the program of unemployment insurance which lacked this element, indispensable to human dignity.
I am happy to note that the speech from the throne deals at length with world peace and assistance to underdeveloped countries. To raise the standard of living of needy people is surely the worthiest and noblest contribution to the maintenance of world peace. It is essential in this era of interdependence. And it is at the same time and above all to achieve a humane purpose. Are these not sufficient reasons to prompt us to an even greater contribution?
Mr. Speaker, it is on this most peaceful note that I move, seconded by the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury):
That the following address be presented to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada:
To His Excellency General the Right Honourable Georges P. Vanier, Companion of the Distinguished Service Order, upon whom has been conferred the Military Cross and the Canadian Forces' Decoration, Governor General and Commander-in-Chief of Canada.
May it please Your Excellency:
We, Her Majesty's most loyal and dutiful subjects, the House of Commons of Canada, in parliament assembled, beg leave to offer our humble thanks to Your Excellency for the gracious speech which Your Excellency has addressed to both Houses of Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, it is for me a moving and
January 19, 1966	COMMONS
memorable experience to have been so warmly greeted by my colleagues on both sides of the house and to share with my colleague from Dollard (Mr. Goyer) the rare honour of speaking for the first time at the very beginning of this twenty seventh parliament.
As he did, Mr. Speaker, I congratulate you and the other officials of the house, the new ministers, the new parliamentary secretaries and all the new members with whom it is my pleasure to sit in this house.

Mr. Speaker, it was with a feeling compounded of admiration and envy that I listened to my colleague, the mover of the Address, speak so fluently and eloquently in both official languages of our country. His facility with my native tongue makes me all the more determined to master his. With the help and patience of my French speaking colleagues I hope I may be able to do greater justice to their beautiful language, which is my second language, before many sessions of this parliament have passed into history.
On entering this house, as I did yesterday,
I could not help but be inspired by the noble example of His Excellency the Governor General, that ideal embodiment of all that is fine and good and unique in the Canadian people. I am confident that I speak for all members when I say that his distinguished presence in the office of Governor General enriches this nation and our pride in it.
We have real cause for pride, too, in the person of our Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), to whom I offer the warmest congratulations on his well earned return to his accustomed place in this house. His high statesmanship, his courage in tackling tough problems and his genius for finding solutions, his integrity nonpareil-these qualities have served and now serve Canada and the world well at an hour when no less would have been enough. I pray that they will serve us still for many years to come.
A newly elected member of parliament, I suppose-and even his family-aspires to some degree of sophistication and aplomb in keeping with the dignity of his office. However, I assure you, Sir, that there is precious little left of one's aplomb when the Prime Minister calls one's home between the meat loaf and the ice cream. I must say it does wonders by way of quieting the clatter of children, and my wife has asked me to request that the Prime Minister call every night at dinner time, particularly while their father is away at Ottawa.

I thank the Prime Minister and his cabinet colleagues most sincerely on behalf of my constituents as well as myself for the honour they have done us in asking me to second the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. It is an appropriate tribute to York-Scarborough, Canada's most populous constituency and in many ways a Canada in miniature, although not very miniature at that. It is, most importantly, the birthplace of our Prime Minister. It has drawn its people from all parts of Canada and the world. The site of many Indian villages in past centuries, first explored by Etienne Brule, settled by families of both French and British stock and now enriched by every race, York-Scarborough is a thick slice of Canada, a very thick slice indeed.
Today it is mainly suburban but embraces city and farm, industry and commerce large and small, people of great wealth and little means. It comprises roughly the northeast quadrant of metropolitan Toronto, including large parts of the township of North York and the town of Leaside as well as most of the township of Scarborough. Beyond to the north it takes in parts of the township and the village of Markham. It was represented in the last house by Maurice J. Moreau, who made an outstanding contribution to the work of parliament. I feel honoured to succeed him.
The present riding was created in 1953, a product of the last redistribution, and an uncommonly healthy child it has been. I will be careful to avoid saying, as one of my predecessors in another party incautiously said in this house, that York-Scarborough is inadequately represented here. Such a statement is open to dangerous misinterpretation. Perhaps I should say that quantitatively the parliamentary representation of the people of York-Scarborough is wildly inequitable.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
It is impossible to avoid comparisons when speaking of York-Scarborough. I know my colleagues will understand that when I draw comparisons it is with no intent to minimize the importance of other ridings and regions but only to do some small measure of justice to my own. It would be difficult for me to exaggerate, because York-Scarborough is a living exaggeration of the flaws in our existing electoral machinery. I am grateful that it will not outlive this parliament.
Meanwhile, it is gargantuan and growing at a pace probably unexcelled in North America. There are those who, with good cause if no constitutional basis, refer to my
January 19, 1966

The Address-Mr. Stanbury constituency as the province of York-Scarborough. On its last voters list-and I trust it will be its last-there were almost 191,000 electors. With a population of well over 300,000 it is truly a province among ridings. For its representative it is rather sobering to realize that York-Scarborough has twice as many residents as live in one province and the territories combined, and about as many people as are represented in this house by a dozen members together.
Mine is not the only part of Canada which has had to endure, still endures, and must endure until the end of this parliament, increasingly acute under-representation. It is just the most hideous example. I understand we are to receive imminently the report of the Representation Commissioner. I sincerely hope it is farsighted enough to ensure that areas of rapid growth such as York-Scar-borough have fair representation between the next election and the next redistribution. At least we know, as a result of the Government's action in the last parliament, that redistribution hereafter will follow quickly on the heels of each decennial census. So there is never likely to be another riding like the York-Scarborough of today. But meanwhile York-Scarborough and the inequity of its representation will continue to grow by leaps and bounds, a grotesque distortion of the democratic process.
In the circumstances, it would not surprise me to hear rumblings of an unquiet revolution in the province of York-Scarborough- that the concession roads of Markham are blocked by tractors, that the acting treasurer of North York has been dispatching notes to foreign powers, that the lovely lady Mayor of Leaside craves a bank of her own, and that the Scarborough township solicitor has sharp words prepared for the next Federal-Provincial conference.
I trust these things will not come to pass. But if they did it would not be the first time the people of my constituency have risen up in defence of their right to representative and responsible government. The history of the area rings with the clamour of William Lyon Mackenzie's rebels marching into muddy York to beard the Family Compact. York-Scarborough shares with adjoining ridings of today the Liberal heritage of Mackenzie, Mulock and King. From Thornhill and Markham at the north to Lake Ontario's majestic bluffs, from historic Yonge Street on the west to Pickering township on the east, York-Scarborough is rich in its past, its present and, most of all, its future.


As much as any other part of this nation, perhaps, York-Scarborough represents the shape of Canada's future. It is a laboratory of the break-neck urbanization which is so changing the face of our nation that by the end of this century almost half of all Canadians will probably live in nine large cities and 90 per cent of our people will be urban dwellers. Today the complex forces of explosive population growth and urbanization can be seen at work in our metropolitan areas. Tomorrow these local growing pains may be a national malady if they are not studied and mastered on a national scale. Might it not soon be time for a department of urban affairs to define national objectives for urban development, redevelopment and housing, to expand research and establish policies and programs for all Canada which will mould the best physical, fiscal and human qualities into our evolving communities? I feel that a concentrated federal effort may be needed to ensure for future generations a meaningful environment in the urban Canada or tomorrow.
The quality of life for our children and our children's children must surely be the prime concern of government. I believe the people of York-Scarborough are concerned with this above all and in that way as in many others they are typical of Canadians everywhere. Of all York-Scarborough's wealth the greatest is its children. No part of Canada, I am sure, is more generously endowed with this most precious natural resource. Ours is a riding, generally speaking, of young families much like my own, with several small children and at least one large mortgage. To us in York-Scarborough, therefore, education is of paramount interest. I am convinced that it must now be a paramount concern of the nation, and I am delighted that the Throne Speech indicates that the Government so regards it.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY MOVED BY MR. J. P. GOYER AND SECONDED BY MR. ROBERT STANBURY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY MOVED BY MR. J. P. GOYER AND SECONDED BY MR. ROBERT STANBURY
speechtext:
Although education in
Canada is primarily a provincial responsibility, it has become clearer and clearer in recent years that both the provincial and the national interests demand active federal participation in this field. I am happy that great strides have been made and are being made to bring the federal and provincial governments into close partnership for the advancement of educational opportunity for all Canadians. No federal Government has interested itself so sincerely or committed itself so deeply to the task of meeting the nation's educational needs as has the present one. Provincial governments, by and large, seem
January 19, 19G6

to be recognizing the need for partnership and welcoming federal participation in the assault on the country's educational problems. Any other attitude would, I suggest, be criminally self-centred in the Canada of today whose very future as a nation is hitched to the education star.
I feel strongly that there should be a coordinated and concentrated national effort, fully recognizing the priority of the provinces but focusing the nation's attention and resources on education as the most basic and vital of factors in our national growth and well-being. I believe an office of education in a federal department would serve this purpose, co-ordinating the many existing federal education functions, and working closely with the provinces in establishing national goals and standards. Many new programs of national value could be undertaken jointly under the stimulus of such an office. The government has recognized, and we must face the fact, that Canada is still an underdeveloped country in the field of human resources. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that Canada has suffered too long from the lack of sharp national focus on education. Without it we may suffer tragically as a nation in the crucial years immediately ahead.
Ahead, just over the horizon, lies the dawn of Canada's second century. It is a century which will belong to the youth of today, the young people of Canada who, I believe, must be better prepared and motivated to mould it, move it and improve it than has been any previous generation. I believe they are. Perhaps my view of the recent election was distorted by my personal involvement. However, I was impressed with the avid interest of young people as I had never been aware of it before.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
It may be partly a product of parental example, because in York-Scarborough there has always been a high degree of interest in public affairs. Generally, about 80 per cent of the electorate there vote in federal elections. But I think more likely it is indicative of a general interest and concern among young Canadians. I am glad they will have the opportunity for service in the Company of Young Canadians which I believe they will eagerly welcome. I hope many more of them, aged 18 and over, will have the opportunity to vote in the next federal election.
If youth's interest in politics is growing, so is its concern, and rightly so. I believe there is cause for concern that our politics have not kept pace with the times, that retention or
The Address-Mr. Stanbury attainment of office is no longer an adequate goal of a political party, that Parliament has too much to do to be embroiled constantly in fractious partisan infighting, that if we practice stagecoach politics in the space age we will ourselves be regarded as tragic anachronisms.
I am encouraged by the evident general acceptance of the need for further reforming the procedures of this House to make it a more productive instrument of the public will and the public good. But the real and meaningful reform must surely be in our attitudes and actions. If they are constructive we will restore and justify Canadians' confidence in the ancient and hallowed institution of parliament. If they are not we could irrevocably damage it. We all want to guard jealously our rights and privileges, to speak and be heard, to support and oppose, but I hope we will keep firmly in mind the duty and the responsibility which accompany those rights and privileges.
Young people, and all Canadians, have a right to expect that this will be a parliament which will get things done. We have much to do. I am glad we will be asked to press ahead with an ever wider-ranging attack on poverty in this nation of plenty, to adopt a distinctively Canadian national anthem, to commit massive funds to increase educational opportunity and stimulate research, to advance toward a national medicare plan in co-operation with the provinces, to shoulder our fair share of international responsibilities, to establish a Canada Development Corporation to give Canadians fresh means and new incentive to invest in our own future.
All the things which need doing cannot be done in this session. But if I may offer my personal capsule speech from the backbench, I hope we can soon accomplish reform of our archaic divorce and birth control laws; that we can abolish capital punishment; that we can take giant steps toward full justice for our first citizens, our Indians and Eskimos; that we can continue to work toward the freest possible access to the best possible education at all levels for all Canadians.
Our nation's problems are not small nor few. But neither are its resources. No country in the world is more fortunate in its geography, its gifts of nature, its friends and its people. What we see today as Canada's central problems are also its unique advantages: a rich continent to be shared and a diverse, distinctive culture to be cherished. These are challenges to be faced and met, not calamities
January 19, 1966

The Address-Mr. Stanbury to bemoan. Under the leadership of the Prime Minister I know we will rise to these challenges and nourish our unique Canadian identity while strengthening our national unity.
The program which has been placed before us in the Speech from the Throne is a challenging and creative one, one which looks over the horizon and beyond to create new and broader opportunities for all Canadians. It is a program of new horizons, a worthy blueprint for the first session of a centennial parliament which will carry our country out
of its first century and into a new one glowing with promise. It will be our duty, our challenge, our mission, to build from this blueprint a better Canada in a better world.
So, Mr. Speaker, I take great pleasure in seconding the motion of my hon. friend, the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Goyer), and commending it to your consideration.
